dialogs.intro: Saturday market in Utrecht. Budi is standing at the cheese stall.

notes: **Zegt u het maar** is the most typical stallholder's greeting in the Netherlands — literally "just say it", meaning "what would you like?". At the bakery you'll also hear *Wie is er aan de beurt?* (whose turn is it?).
**Twaalf euro vijftig** = €12.50 (written €12,50 in Dutch). Cents aren't read as "point fifty": you just say the euros and then the cents. For a round price people simply say *twaalf euro*.

**Een pondje** — in the Netherlands *een pond* means **500 grams**, not an English pound. Together with *een ons* (100 grams!) it's a leftover from the old measuring system that is still very much alive at markets and cheese shops. Ask for *twee ons kaas* and you'll get 200 grams.
**Vijfenzestig or zesenvijftig?** You will really run into this confusion, not just in the book. The key: **the units come first**, then *en*, then the tens. So *vijf-en-zestig* = 5 and 60 = 65.
**Bij ons** = "where we come from", a short way to refer to your own country or culture.
**Nog iets erbij?** = "anything else?" The closing answer: *Nee, dat was het* (no, that's all) — a sentence you'll use almost every day.
**Dan is het rond** — the stallholder rounds down. Haggling isn't usual in the Netherlands, but near closing time prices often drop on their own.

grammars.title: Numbers: units first, then tens
body: From 21 to 99, Dutch says **the units first** and joins them with *en*. German does the same; modern English doesn't (though old English did: "four-and-twenty blackbirds"). This is the only part of the Dutch number system that needs serious practice.
after: They are all written **as one word**, however long. The two dots over a letter (*tweeëndertig*, *drieëntwintig*) are just a spelling mark so that *ee* and *e* aren't read as one sound.
The tens: *tien, twintig, dertig, veertig, vijftig, zestig, zeventig, tachtig, negentig*. Note **dertig** and **veertig**, which change shape, and **tachtig**, which starts with a t-.
A listening trick that really helps: as soon as you hear *en* in the middle of a number, hold the first number in your head and wait for the second — the second one is the tens.

grammars.title: Big numbers and how to write them
body: Above a hundred, the order makes sense again.
after: ⚠️ **The dot and the comma swap places** compared with English: Dutch writes a dot for thousands and a comma for decimals. *€ 1.250,75* (= €1,250.75) is read "duizend tweehonderdvijftig euro vijfenzeventig".
The Dutch often count in hundreds instead of thousands for years and prices: *negentienhonderd* (1900, like English "nineteen hundred"), *achttienhonderd euro* (€1,800).
*Honderd* and *duizend* take no *een* in front when they stand alone: *honderd euro* (a hundred euros), not *een honderd euro*.

blocks.title: Money and paying in the Netherlands
items: **Pinnen** (debit card) is the default way to pay. Many shops have an *alleen pinnen* sign — cash isn't accepted at all.
Credit cards are often **not** accepted in supermarkets and small restaurants; a debit card (Maestro/V-Pay) is what works.
1- and 2-cent coins aren't used: cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5 cents. Card payments aren't rounded.
*Statiegeld* — a bottle deposit. Plastic bottles and cans carry a 15-25 cent deposit that you get back by feeding them into the machine at the supermarket.
Giving a *fooi* (tip) isn't required; rounding up is already considered polite.

blocks.text: Dutch phone numbers are read **in pairs**, not digit by digit as many English speakers would. This throws beginners into a panic on the phone — and since each pair is read backwards, a pair can sound like two other digits. It's perfectly fine to ask: *Kunt u het cijfer voor cijfer zeggen?* ("Could you say it digit by digit?").
A Dutch postcode (four digits + two letters) is almost a full address: together with the house number, it's enough to fill in nearly any online form. Learn your postcode in your first week.
